unit_label: Module B unit 6 (courseware unit 15): Conflict Management and Negotiation

facts.statement: Conflict can be expressed in insults, non-cooperation, bullying and anger; causes range from personality clashes to misunderstood communication to organisational mismanagement; its negative effects include work disruption, decreased productivity, project failure, absenteeism, turnover and termination; emotional stress can be both a cause and an effect. Conflict at work cannot be avoided altogether but should be managed and resolved. Employees engaged in conflict lose concentration and interest, so goals are not achieved. The employer's role, exercised by managers and HR professionals, is to develop a workplace culture designed to prevent conflict, resting on fairness, trust and mutual respect at all levels. Conflict is more harmful in service organisations such as banks, which are custodians of public money, so conflict management should be assigned to executives with the required skill, ability and strategy, and the executive's performance in handling it should be one of the key performance indicators in the appraisal system.

Conflict is a sharp disagreement or opposition of interests or ideas; it occurs whenever individuals or groups have different values, opinions, needs and interests and cannot find a middle way. The courseware quotes the Oxford Learners Dictionary (a situation in which people, groups or countries disagree strongly or are involved in a serious argument) and McLean (2005) (the physical or psychological struggle associated with the perception of opposing incompatible goals, desires, demands, wants or needs), and itself defines conflict as a clash between individuals arising out of a difference in thought process, attitudes, understanding, interests, requirements and even perceptions. Conflict is a normal part of any relationship; the key is not to fear or avoid it but to resolve it in a healthy way; how conflict is handled influences, reinforces or destroys the relationship. It can be an opportunity for clarification and healthy growth when managed respectfully, and it is better to identify it early. Experts differ in their ideas of it: as a natural phenomenon, as obstructive behaviour, or as an excuse for goal incompatibility.

Conflict at the workplace lowers team morale, raises absenteeism and so reduces productivity; it is the struggle that happens when people feel they have incompatible goals, wants, demands or needs. It has been estimated (the courseware says) that managers spend at least 25 per cent of their time resolving workplace conflicts. The most common response is flight or fight; either way people feel dissatisfied because no resolution is achieved. Conflict is inevitable but can be managed by handling disagreements, misunderstandings and struggles with an open mind and a positive approach; advice includes listening carefully, compromising and discussing with the team, avoiding unnecessary fault-finding, remaining calm and composed, and adopting a professional approach.

Hocker and Wilmot (1991) offer principles that describe conflict: it is universal; associated with incompatible goals; associated with scarce resources; associated with interference; not a sign of a poor relationship; cannot be avoided; cannot always be resolved; and is not always bad. The main characteristics summarised by the courseware are: conflict involves opposition; it is more than a disagreement (one or both parties perceive a threat, real or imagined); the response to conflict is based on perceptions influenced by life experiences, cultures, values and beliefs rather than an objective review of facts; it is inevitable (diverse employees, views and work styles); it will always remain among humans; it cannot be avoided; and it is an opportunity for growth, because once resolved it helps build trust. It is also described as a process that begins with one party perceiving the other to oppose or negatively affect its interests and ends with competing, collaborating, compromising or avoiding.

Three viewpoints on whether conflict is bad: traditionalists believe conflict is bad and should be avoided; human relations experts feel it is natural and gives an avenue to know opinions and an opportunity for creativity and persuasion, calling for an open approach; integrationists view conflict as inevitable and helpful, a positive force except when misdiagnosed, mismanaged or improperly avoided. The key to conflict resolution is its proper diagnosis and resolution.
facts.locator: Printed p. 344, Are Conflicts Bad and/or Undesirable?

facts.statement: Organisational conflict is disagreement between groups or employees about work-related issues, in three main types. Task conflict involves differences on work details and goals (duties, expectations, assignments, sharing of resources, procedures and policies, interpretation of facts); it is the easiest to solve, and excellent communication, employee debate and active listening usually find the remedy; it can cause good discussion and streamline productivity channels, and the best way to resolve it is collaborative problem solving, with solutions found jointly rather than imposed. Relationship conflict is personal, over personal issues not work-related, arising from differences in personality, style, taste and working styles; it can be the most difficult to diffuse and resolve, can be long lasting and hurts job commitment, productivity, trust and work performance, and is resolved by listening to the other person's point of view and showing empathy and interest. Value conflict arises from fundamental differences in life experiences, cultures, identities, values and beliefs (politics, religion, ethics, norms) and can arise in work decisions and policies; according to Susskind, disputes involving values heighten defensiveness, distrust and alienation, and instead of resolving a values-based dispute one should move beyond demonisation towards mutual understanding and respect through dialogue, with a cognitive understanding of the other's point of view that does not require sympathy or emotional connection.

Intra-individual (intra-personal) conflict arises when an individual's objective differs from the company's vision, from frustration, from numerous roles demanding equal attention, and from goals with both negative and positive aspects. Goal conflict occurs when attaining one goal excludes attaining another; three forms are approach-approach (two or more positive but mutually exclusive goals), approach-avoidance (one goal that contains both positive and negative characteristics) and avoidance-avoidance (two or more negative but mutually exclusive goals). Frustration occurs when a motivated drive is blocked before a person reaches the goal, by external barriers (non-social such as floods or breakdown of transport, or social) or internal barriers (personal limitations, lack of skill or intelligence), which are more lasting; frustrated individuals adopt aggression, withdrawal, fixation or compromise (aggression is attacking the barrier, withdrawal is backing away, fixation is continuing efforts to break the barrier and compromise is the search for a new goal). Role conflict arises from the need to play several roles at once with inadequate time and resources; the courseware lists three types: person-role conflict (between the person's personality and the expectations of the role), intra-role conflict (contradictory expectations about how a given role should be played) and inter-role conflict (differing requirements of two or more roles played at the same time, such as work and non-work roles).

Reasons for conflict: misunderstanding, lack of communication and disagreement; differences in values, motivations, perceptions, ideas or desires, behind which a deep personal need often lies; ego, which makes conflict a win-lose situation in which the "losers" resist and retaliate. The courseware lists common causes at work: resistance to change (fear of the unknown; computerisation in banks led to conflicts at various levels in the early stages; management should guide employees through change); work habits (for example being extra diligent and rechecking files); poor communication (different communication styles; open communication avoids this); personality clashes (managers should consider both viewpoints); poor performance (not addressed; training needed); poor supervision (incompetent or biased supervisors who listen to only one side); and other reasons: economics (insufficient remuneration), stress from working conditions, weak leadership, poor organisational structure and lack of teamwork, status (a "wrong" person promoted), power struggle, incongruence (an employee required to do something beyond his or her liking or interests) and lack of transparency at management level.

A conflict has five phases: the prelude phase (all the factors that possibly cause conflict: lack of coordination, differences in interests, dissimilarity in culture, religion or education); the triggering phase (an event that triggers the conflict); the initiation phase (the conflict has begun: heated arguments, abuses and verbal disagreements are warnings); the differentiation phase (individuals voice their differences and the reasons for the conflict are raised); and the resolution phase (the various options to resolve are explored and individuals reconcile and compromise to some extent).

Conflict resolution handled in a healthy way increases understanding, builds trust and strengthens relationships; resolving it constructively can turn a destructive situation into an opportunity for growth, creativity and enhanced performance; it is the duty of management to resolve it. The easiest three-step formula is: listen (active listening is important), talk (clear and open communication) and resolve. The Helpguide.org team's process: listen for what is felt as well as said; make conflict resolution the priority rather than winning or being right; focus on the present; pick your battles; be willing to forgive; and agree to disagree.

The Thomas-Kilmann model identifies five approaches to resolving conflict: avoiding (ignoring or sidestepping the conflict in the hope that it dissolves), accommodating (satisfying the other party's concerns at the expense of one's own), compromising (finding an acceptable resolution that partly but not entirely satisfies all parties), competing (satisfying one's own desires at the expense of the others) and collaborating (finding a solution that entirely satisfies the concerns of all the parties). The two dimensions are assertiveness (taking action to satisfy one's own needs) and cooperativeness (taking action to satisfy the other's needs); each strategy involves different degrees of both. Conflict resolution can take passive forms such as avoiding the issue when one person lets the other make the decision.

A five-step conflict resolution process: (1) find out the source of the conflict, using questions and giving both parties a chance to tell their side; (2) look beyond: the cause is often the individual's point of view, and the source may be a minor earlier issue, so probe beyond the triggering incident; (3) take suggestions for solution from each party, steering the discussion from finger pointing to ways of resolving it; (4) identify acceptable solutions, pointing out the merits of ideas from each perspective and for the organisation, and suggesting the need for cooperation; and (5) final agreement: the manager gets the two parties to accept one of the alternatives, aiming at a mutually accepted agreement, sometimes in a written contract with actions and timeframes. The process may work between groups as well as individuals.

In most conflicts neither party is right or wrong; different perceptions collide, and the organisation should respond quickly and professionally. Conflict management is the approach and strategy geared towards achieving a positive outcome among the parties; it should aim at minimising affective conflicts at all levels, attaining and maintaining a moderate amount of substantive conflict, and matching the status and concerns of the parties. Styles of conflict management behaviour: Mary Parker Follett described domination, compromise and integration (integration involves openness, exchanging information, looking for alternatives and examining differences to solve the problem in a manner acceptable to both parties); Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton presented five styles: forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising and problem solving; no style is applicable in all situations. A manager should not avoid a conflict hoping it will go away; should ask participants to describe specific actions they want the other party to take; may involve a third party (a non-direct superior with access to the situation); and should not meet the parties separately only.

Actions a manager can take to minimise conflicts: regular review of job descriptions; establishing rapport and relationships with all subordinates by meeting at regular intervals; regular progress reports; training in interpersonal communication, conflict management and delegation of authority; mutual development of procedures (inputs from employees, written procedures distributed to all); regular management meetings; and a suggestion box. Elements of a conflict management policy and process: acknowledge that a difficult situation may exist; allow individuals to express their feelings; understand and define the problem; determine the underlying need (looking for needs rather than solutions); find common areas of agreement, no matter how small (agree on the problem, procedure, worst fears and a small change); find solutions to satisfy needs by generating multiple alternatives, determining actions and making sure the parties agree (total silence may be a sign of passive resistance); follow up to monitor actions (a follow-up meeting in one or two weeks); and decide what to do if the conflict remains unresolved (an outside facilitator or expert, or treating it as a performance issue for coaching, appraisal or disciplinary action).

facts.statement: Negotiation is useful when two individuals have a similar objective but conflict on how it is reached; conflict resolution is the process of resolving a dispute by meeting at least some of each side's needs and addressing their interests, and sometimes requires both a power-based and an interest-based approach. Power used to control, intimidate or force solutions adds to the grounds for future conflict. Negotiation is communication focused on finding an agreement that addresses the concerns of parties who want different outcomes. Common situations: conflicts between employees (a primary duty of supervisors and managers), compensation (agreeing a mutually acceptable rate), disputes between a business and the public (a dissatisfied customer) and disagreements during collaboration (project teams over limited resources or how to approach a client request).

The courseware lists eleven skills and strategies for resolving conflicts through negotiation: effective communication skills (polite and convincing speech, no shouting, no abusive language); listening skills (active listening by repeating back critical information, reaffirming statements and maintaining eye contact; do not jump to conclusions); discussion (open forum, invite everyone involved); patience; impartiality; never criticise (guide the other person and make him realise his mistakes); positive attitude (do not play the blame game, avoid backbiting); address the conflict, not the person (avoid personal attacks); find shared interests (redefine the issue so both sides can achieve a win, however small, and develop a win-win situation); set an objective (such as a price that provides value for the client and profit for the company); and determine the Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA), including the opposing negotiator's BATNA, which may offer an opportunity to reduce conflict and promote compromise. Effective negotiation is a two-way process that encourages both sides to participate, and the golden rule is to attain a win-win situation; win-lose and lose-lose outcomes are not congenial.

(The courseware says managers spend at least a quarter of their time on conflicts; this figure is not verified.)

| **Inevitable** | Diverse people with different views and work styles |
| **An opportunity for growth** | Once resolved it builds trust and confidence in the relationship |

payload.title: Conflict within an individual: goal, frustration and role conflict
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Intra-individual** (intra-personal) conflict arises when a person's objectives differ from the company's vision, from frustration, from roles that demand equal attention, and from goals with positive and negative features.

**Goal conflict** (attaining one goal excludes another):

| Form | Choice between |
| --- | --- |
| **Approach-approach** | Two or more **positive**, mutually exclusive goals |
| **Approach-avoidance** | A single goal with **both** positive and negative features |
| **Avoidance-avoidance** | Two or more **negative**, mutually exclusive goals |

**Frustration:** a motivated drive is **blocked** before the goal is reached, by external barriers (non-social such as power failures or transport breakdown; or social) or internal ones (limitations, lack of skill; more lasting). | **Inter-role** | Differing requirements of **two or more** roles played at the same time |

payload.title: Why conflicts arise at work
payload.core_explanation_md:
Behind most conflicts lie **misunderstandings, poor communication and disagreement**, often with a deep personal need underneath (to feel safe, respected or valued). **Ego** turns conflict into **win-lose**, and the "losers" resist and retaliate.

| Cause | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Resistance to change** | Fear of the unknown; for example early computerisation in banks |
| **Work habits** | For example being over-diligent and rechecking files |
| **Poor communication** | Different styles; silence drives conflict underground |
| **Personality clashes** | Differences in attitudes, values, goals and perceptions |
| **Poor performance** | Not addressed; training needed |
| **Poor supervision** | Incompetent or biased supervisors who hear one side |
| **Economics** | Insufficient remuneration |
| **Stress; weak leadership; poor structure; no teamwork** | Working conditions, less qualified leader, unclear organisation |
| **Status; power struggle** | A "wrong" person promoted; everyone wants to lead |
| **Incongruence** | Required to do something against one's liking or interests |
| **Lack of transparency** | At management level |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Management should guide employees through change by explaining the reasons behind it and what it means for them.

payload.title: The five phases of a conflict
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Prelude** | The background factors: lack of coordination, differing interests, cultural, religious or educational dissimilarity |
| 2. **Triggering** | An **event** sets the conflict off (no conflict arises on its own) |
| 3. **Initiation** | The conflict has begun: heated arguments, abuse, verbal disagreement are warning signs |
| 4. **Differentiation** | The parties **voice their differences** and the reasons are raised |
| 5. **Resolution** | Options are explored; people reconcile and compromise to some extent |

The earlier a conflict is spotted, the easier to resolve. The courseware's advice: talk and discuss rather than continue the fight.

payload.title: Resolving conflict: listen, talk, resolve; and the Thomas-Kilmann styles
payload.core_explanation_md:
Resolved in a healthy way, conflict **builds understanding and trust**; constructively resolved, it can turn a destructive situation into **growth, creativity and better performance**. The courseware's easiest formula: **Listen, Talk, Resolve**. The Helpguide.org team adds: listen for what is **felt** as well as said; make **resolution** the priority rather than winning or being right; **focus on the present**; **pick your battles**; **be willing to forgive**; **agree to disagree**.

**Thomas-Kilmann model:** five approaches on two dimensions, **assertiveness** (satisfying your own needs) and **cooperativeness** (satisfying the other's):

| Approach | Meaning | Assertiveness / cooperativeness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Avoiding** | Ignore or sidestep the conflict | Low / low |
| **Accommodating** | Satisfy the other's concerns at your own expense | Low / high |
| **Competing** | Satisfy your desires at the others' expense | High / low |
| **Collaborating** | A solution that fully satisfies all parties | High / high |
| **Compromising** | A partial satisfaction for all | Medium / medium |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Collaborating takes the most time but gives the best result when the issue matters to both sides; avoiding is sensible only when the issue is trivial or the timing is wrong.

payload.title: The five-step resolution process for a manager
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. **Find the source**: ask questions ("Why are you so upset?", "How did this begin?") and give **both** parties a chance to tell their story; acknowledge what you hear.
2. **Look beyond**: the cause is often the person's point of view, or a minor old issue grown with stress; probe beyond the triggering incident.
3. **Take suggestions** from each party on how things could change; steer away from **finger-pointing** and towards solutions.
4. **Identify acceptable solutions**: point out the merits of ideas from each perspective and for the organisation, and suggest the need for **cooperation**.
5. **Final agreement**: get both parties to accept one alternative; aim for a **mutually accepted** agreement, sometimes written with actions and timeframes.

It works between **groups** as well as individuals.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Impartiality matters: listening to both sides shows the manager is not taking one.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Find out the source of the conflict by asking questions and giving both parties a chance to tell their side.

payload.title: Managing conflict: styles and what a manager can do
payload.core_explanation_md:
In most conflicts **neither party is simply right**: different perceptions collide. Conflict management aims at **minimising affective conflict** (about feelings and relationships) at all levels and keeping a **moderate amount of substantive conflict** (about the work).

**Styles** the courseware names:

| Author | Styles |
| --- | --- |
| **Follett** | Domination, compromise, **integration** (open exchange to find a solution acceptable to both) |
| **Blake and Mouton** | Forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising, problem solving |

No style fits every situation.

**Do not** avoid a conflict hoping it will go away. Ask participants to describe the **specific actions** they want from the other party; consider a **third party** (a non-direct superior with access to the situation).

**Preventive actions:** regular review of **job descriptions**; **rapport** with subordinates; regular **reports**; **training** in communication, conflict management and delegation; **mutual development of procedures**; regular **meetings**; a **suggestion box**.

**Policy elements:** acknowledge the problem; let people express feelings; define the problem; find the **underlying need**; find **common ground**, however small; find solutions that satisfy needs (silence may be passive resistance); **follow up**; and if unresolved, use an **outside facilitator** or treat it as a **performance issue**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Looking for needs rather than solutions is described as a powerful tool: once you know why each party wants what it wants, there is more room to find a solution both can live with.

payload.title: Negotiation for resolving conflicts
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Negotiation** is communication aimed at an agreement that addresses the concerns of parties who want **different outcomes**. It helps when two people share an objective but disagree on how to reach it. **Conflict resolution** means meeting at least some of each side's needs and interests; it may need both **power-based** and **interest-based** approaches, but force and intimidation **add to the grounds for future conflict**.

Common situations: **conflicts between employees** (a main duty of supervisors), **compensation**, **disputes with the public** (a dissatisfied customer) and **disagreements in collaboration** (limited resources, approach to a client).

**Eleven skills and strategies:**

1. Effective communication (polite, specific, no shouting)
2. Listening (repeat back, reaffirm, eye contact)
3. Discussion (open, invite all involved)
4. Patience
5. Impartiality
6. Never criticise (guide the other person)
7. Positive attitude (no blame game, no backbiting)
8. **Address the conflict, not the person**
9. **Find shared interests**
10. **Set an objective**
11. Know your **BATNA** (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement), and the other side's

**Golden rule:** aim for **win-win**. Win-lose and lose-lose outcomes do not resolve the conflict.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away: you will not accept a deal worse than your best alternative.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Fixation is continuing efforts to break the barrier.

payload.stem_md: A branch manager is expected both to cut costs and to increase staff, so the demands on the same role contradict. This is

options.explanation_md: This is between personality and role.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Contradictory expectations within one role are intra-role conflict.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is described as a cause of conflict by "resistance to change"?

options.text_md: Employees' fear of the unknown, as with early computerisation in banks

payload.correct_explanation_md: Fear of the unknown leads to resistance to change, as with computerisation.

payload.stem_md: A supervisor who listens to only one side of a dispute is an example of which cause of conflict?

options.text_md: Lack of transparency at management level

payload.correct_explanation_md: Biased supervisors who listen to only one side cause conflict.

payload.stem_md: In a conflict that becomes a "win-lose" situation because of ego, the courseware says the "losers" will

options.text_md: Defy, test, resist and retaliate against the "winners"
options.explanation_md: One-sidedness raises the chance of more conflict.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The losers will defy, test, resist and retaliate, so conflict recurs.

payload.stem_md: Which phase of conflict is the one in which an event sets the conflict off?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The triggering phase is the event that sets off the conflict.

payload.stem_md: In which phase do the parties voice their differences and raise the reasons for the conflict?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The differentiation phase is when the parties voice their differences.

payload.stem_md: The easiest three-step formula for resolving conflict in the courseware is
payload.correct_explanation_md: The formula is listen, talk, resolve.

payload.stem_md: In the Thomas-Kilmann model, trying to satisfy the other party's concerns at the expense of one's own is called

options.explanation_md: The other's needs are put first.
One's own desires are put first.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Accommodating means satisfying the other party at your own expense.

payload.stem_md: Finding a solution that entirely satisfies the concerns of all the parties is the approach of

options.explanation_md: It looks for a full win-win.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Collaborating seeks a solution that entirely satisfies all parties.

payload.stem_md: Which pair correctly gives the two dimensions of the Thomas-Kilmann model?

options.explanation_md: These are forms of goal conflict.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The dimensions are assertiveness (own needs) and cooperativeness (other's needs).

payload.stem_md: In the five-step conflict resolution process, the last step is

options.text_md: Find out the source of the conflict
Final agreement, accepted by both parties, sometimes in writing

payload.correct_explanation_md: The fifth step is a final, mutually accepted agreement.

payload.stem_md: Mary Parker Follett described the styles of handling conflict as

options.text_md: Forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising and problem solving
options.explanation_md: These are Blake and Mouton's five.

options.text_md: Avoiding, accommodating, compromising, competing and collaborating

options.explanation_md: This is the courseware's easy formula.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Follett's styles are domination, compromise and integration.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is a preventive action a manager can take to minimise conflicts?

options.explanation_md: Rapport should be built with all subordinates.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Regular review of job descriptions is one of the listed actions.

payload.stem_md: In framing a conflict management process, why is "total silence" after proposed actions seen as a warning?

options.text_md: It shows the problem has been resolved
It may be a sign of passive resistance, so real agreement must be sought

payload.correct_explanation_md: Silence can be passive resistance; real agreement is needed from everyone.

payload.stem_md: In negotiation, BATNA stands for

options.text_md: Bank Authority for Treasury Negotiation Approval
Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement

payload.correct_explanation_md: BATNA is the Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement.

payload.stem_md: The "golden rule" of negotiation in the courseware is to

options.text_md: Attain a win-win situation in which both parties feel they achieved something worthwhile

payload.correct_explanation_md: The golden rule is to attain a win-win outcome.

payload.stem_md: Which skill means focusing attention on the issue rather than responding to personal attacks?

options.text_md: Address the conflict, not the person

options.explanation_md: This is about a target outcome.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Address the conflict, not the person.

payload.stem_md: The courseware says that using power to control, intimidate or force solutions on other people

options.text_md: Always ends the conflict for good
Adds to the grounds for future conflict

payload.correct_explanation_md: Forced outcomes only add to the grounds for future conflict.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is a common situation in which conflict negotiation is used, according to the courseware?

options.text_md: A dissatisfied customer who needs a resolution
options.explanation_md: Disputes between a business and the public are a listed situation.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Disputes between a business and the public are a listed negotiation situation.

unresolved: Courseware printed p. 339 (unit title page) was not read in detail; the Check Your Progress questions (printed pp. 359-360) and the terminal questions and further readings were read but not used.

The courseware attributes frameworks to named authors and sources (McLean 2005, Hocker and Wilmot 1991, Marquid cited by Kelley 2006, Susskind, Follett, Blake and Mouton, the Thomas-Kilmann model, the Helpguide.org team); none was checked against the original work. A statement that managers spend at least 25 per cent of their time resolving workplace conflicts is the courseware's and was not checked.

The courseware lists Blake and Mouton's five styles as forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising and problem solving, and the Thomas-Kilmann styles as avoiding, accommodating, compromising, competing and collaborating; it also names Follett's three (domination, compromise, integration). They are taught as the courseware lists them. It also says assertiveness and cooperativeness are the Thomas-Kilmann dimensions but its sentence on the degrees is partly garbled ("competing consists of a low degree of cooperation and a high degree of assertiveness"); the items use the standard placement (competing: high assertiveness, low cooperation; accommodating: low assertiveness, high cooperation; avoiding: low on both; collaborating: high on both; compromising: middle on both).
The courseware's account of the "phases of conflict" and its worked illustration (Ram and Rahim) are used only as the five-phase list.
The courseware's discussion of frustration (aggression, withdrawal, fixation, compromise) is reported as given; no research source is named.
No calculation or regulation is involved; session applicability is not applicable except that the courseware states no cut-off-dated rule.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
